To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the transgenic hybrid sweet gum plants expressing γ-glutathionylcysteinesynthetase or merA gene have enhanced ability to tolerate and remove mercury from contaminated soil and water.
transgenic sweetgum overexpressing ECS and various merA genes can grow in the presence 25–50 μM mercury (as HgCl2) and release Hg(0).
transgenic sweetgum plants constitutively over-expressing merA9 or merA18 genes are resistant to mercury and are capable of releasing Hg(0), which is less toxic to the environment than Hg(II).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of transgenic sweetgum for phytoremeditation of Hg-contaminated soil.
developing transgenic trees that will help remediate mercury pollution.
developing a phytoremediator that is able to remove mercury from contaminated soil and water.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
transgenic sweetgum plants overexpressing mercuric reductive genes are more tolerant to Hg(0), HgCl2 and Hg(II), but transgenic plants overexpressing ECS are not.
the transgenic plants expressing merA9 and ECS are able to grow in mercury-contaminated soils.
transgenic sweetgum overexpressing ECS or merA9 and A18 can grow and tolerate high concentrations of Hg(II), but the transgenic plants are not able to grow to maturity in the presence of Hg(2+).
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transgenic merA plants are more efficient in phytoremediating mercury than the ECS plants, but the ECS plants are more efficient than the wild-type plants.
transgenic sweetgum plants constitutively expressing merA9 and/or merA18 genes have the potential to be used as a phytoremediator of mercury-contaminant soil and/or water.

transgenic sweetgum overexpressing ECS is more resistant to Hg(0), but the plantlet is not able to survive for a long period of time; transgenic merA sweetgum can grow in the presence Hg(II), and releases Hg(0).
The main takeaway from our work is that
transgenic merA plantlet lines are promising for phytoremedial application to remove mercury from contaminated soils and water.
the merA gene is more effective in improving the Hg tolerance of sweetgum than is the ECS gene.

the transgenic merA plantlet lines have the potential for use in phytoremediating mercury-polluted soils and water, and that the ECS transgenic plantlets could be used as a model system for studying the mechanism of phytochelatins-mediated Hg(II)/Cd(II) tolerance.
